questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: recognise the cost of one value stored as many tokens
questions.stem: An intake column records the same single idea as "Y", "yes", "Yes", and 1. What is wrong with the encoding?

options.text: One idea sits under four tokens, so any count of the values silently loses cases
The tokens are too long, so shorter labels would store the answer more cheaply
options.misconception: believes the fault is token width rather than token variety

options.text: The column holds text, and only a numeric column can be counted by any tool
options.misconception: believes text values cannot be counted or grouped at all

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since a spreadsheet counts any distinct value it can see
options.misconception: believes every distinct spelling counts as a distinct answer

questions.explanation: An encoding earns its keep when each value has exactly one token, because then counting, sorting, and filtering all agree. Here the same answer wears four costumes, so a tally of the exact value "Y" under-reports by three quarters of the true total while looking perfectly correct. The tempting answer is C, which mistakes a storage type for a limit: a tool can group text perfectly well, it just groups these four strings as four different answers, which is a data problem, not a tool problem.
questions.hint: Count the true yes answers, then count the cells any single tool would match.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain what a bare code loses without its mapping
questions.stem: A transit dataset stores a line column holding the bare values 1, 2, 3 and ships without any codebook. What has been lost?

options.text: The numbers stand for nothing on their own, since only a mapping gives them meaning
Storage space, because written labels would need more bytes per row than digits
options.misconception: believes a codebook exists to save space rather than to be read

options.text: Sort order, because bare numbers can never be placed in a useful sequence
options.misconception: believes numeric codes cannot be ordered meaningfully

options.text: The ability to filter, because filtering only works on spelled-out words
options.misconception: believes filters require words and refuse numbers

questions.explanation: A code is only interpretable through the mapping that assigns meaning to each value, so a dataset and its codebook travel together or the file is decoration. The numbers are stored perfectly well; what is missing is the sentence that says 1 is the airport spur and 3 is the depot loop, and without it nobody can answer a question about a route. The tempting answer is B, which has the direction backwards: labels are larger, not smaller, and the cost of a missing mapping is not bytes but every future question asked of the data.
questions.hint: Ask what the value 2 tells a reader who has never opened the file.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: reject an ambiguous date encoding
questions.stem: A school register stores each arrival date as the string "3/4/26". Why is that encoding unsafe to rely on?

options.text: It can mean March 4 or April 3, so one string hides two different real days
It uses slashes, which most systems refuse in place of a single separator
options.misconception: believes the separator character causes the date ambiguity

options.text: It drops the century, so a two digit year cannot sit on any calendar
options.misconception: believes a two digit year is the only fault in the string

options.text: It mixes numbers and words, which a date field must never contain
options.misconception: believes the character mix rather than field order is the fault

questions.explanation: An encoding must be unambiguous to a reader who never met the writer. A slash between two numbers that can each be a month leaves the order undetermined, and both readings are ordinary local conventions, so the file cannot even be interpreted until someone guesses. A fixed order with padded numbers removes the choice entirely. The tempting answer is C, which spots a real weakness elsewhere: a two digit year is worth widening, but widening it would leave 3/4/26 just as unreadable as it is now.
questions.hint: Read the string two ways and see whether both readings are ordinary dates.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: identify the type choice that destroys leading zeros
questions.stem: A bus column holds the codes "007", "012", and "021". A teammate saves the file as numbers and the values become 7, 12, and 21. Which decision caused the loss?

options.text: Text that looks like a number was put in a numeric field, so leading zeros dropped
The codes were too short, since six digit codes would have survived the save
options.misconception: believes more padding characters would survive numeric storage

options.text: The columns were saved in the wrong order, which shifted the digits sideways
options.misconception: believes saving to a number column reorders the digits

options.text: The routes were renamed on save, so the old padded names no longer exist
options.misconception: believes the save step renamed the route codes itself

questions.explanation: Choose the storage type from what the value is, not from how it looks. "007" is an identifier, not a quantity: it has no arithmetic meaning and its leading zeros are part of its identity, so a numeric field discards them on the way in. The tempting answer is B, which proposes the wrong repair, because extra zeros inside a numeric field disappear just as thoroughly. Store the code as text, or as a number plus a fixed-width format, and 7 pads back to 007 every time.
questions.hint: Ask whether the code is a quantity you will ever add, or a name you will only compare.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: reject a missing-value marker drawn from inside the data's range
questions.stem: A school stores a weight column where 0 means "no measurement was taken", and 0 is also the true weight of an empty bag. What is the fault?

options.text: 0 is a legal value here, so missing and measured collapse into one indistinguishable group
0 is a number, and a weight column should hold written labels rather than figures
options.misconception: believes a numeric column should store words instead

options.text: 0 is too small for any bag, so it is safe to stand in for a missing reading
options.misconception: believes a value outside any real case is always safe to reuse

options.text: 0 should be stored twice, so the average divides by two for each absent reading
options.misconception: believes duplicating a marker repairs the average it distorts

questions.explanation: A missing-value marker has to sit outside the range of real values, because once it collides with a real reading the collision is unrecoverable later. An empty bag weighs 0, so those rows and the unmeasured rows are the same number, the count of measured bags is wrong, and any average is computed over the wrong denominator. The tempting answer is C is exactly the trap: a marker picked from inside the range always looks safe until someone ships the value that occupies it.
questions.hint: List the real values the column can legitimately hold, then place the marker outside them.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: compute the storage a fixed record layout requires
questions.stem: A school system stores 400 student records. Each record holds 5 fields of 2 bytes each plus a 1-byte marker. How many bytes does the data portion of the file hold?
questions.explanation: One record costs 5 times 2, which is 10 bytes of fields, plus the 1-byte marker, so 11 bytes per record. Across 400 records that is 400 times 11, which is 4400 bytes. The same figure comes from counting the other way: 400 records times 5 fields is 2000 fields, times 2 bytes is 4000 bytes, plus 400 marker bytes is 4400. The tempting 4000 forgets the marker, and a figure built by charging the marker 2 bytes would give 4800.
questions.hint: Work out the cost of one record, then multiply by the number of records.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: see why a free-text field blocks a planned computation
questions.stem: A transit app records each rider's pass type as free text: "senior", "Senior pass", "S/P", "old person's card". What does this block?

options.text: Counting riders by pass type, because a group needs one fixed token per group
File size, because free text holds more characters than a short code would
options.misconception: believes the blocker is file size rather than groupability

options.text: Display, because free text cannot be printed back to riders on screen
options.misconception: believes text values cannot be shown to a reader

options.text: Transparency, because the app hides what it recorded about each rider
options.misconception: believes an unparseable value is a display problem not a data one

questions.explanation: Every question you intend to ask of a field decides how that field has to be encoded, which means the decision belongs before the first row is collected. Counting seniors requires a closed set of tokens, and four free-text variants make every rider their own group. The tempting answer is B, which worries about bytes while the real cost is a broken count; C is simply false, since these strings display fine, and D confuses unreadable-by-machine with hidden-from-human, which are separate problems.
questions.hint: Pick the option naming a question the field could never answer.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: normalise spacing and case before grouping names
questions.stem: A signup list holds "Ruiz", "ruiz", and "Ruiz ", and a group-by produces three groups. Which normalisation collapses them into one?

options.text: Trim the padding and fix the case, so all three entries produce one key
Delete the duplicates, which removes the two odd spellings from the file
options.misconception: believes dropping rows is the same as normalising what remains

options.text: Add a note column, which records that the three entries name one person
options.misconception: believes a comment column changes how software groups values

options.text: Sort the list, which places the two odd spellings beside the correct one
options.misconception: believes visual adjacency changes what a group-by returns

questions.explanation: Normalise before you group, because grouping compares strings exactly and no amount of care in the tool will fix an inconsistent key. A trailing space or a lowercase first letter is a different string, so three groups is the correct answer to a badly keyed question. The tempting answer is B, which destroys evidence instead of repairing the encoding: deleting rows throws away a real signup, while trimming and case-folding keep every row and let the count be right.
questions.hint: Compare the three entries character by character and find the differences.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: judge which unit normalisation is sound before averaging
questions.stem: A food-bank column mixes "2.5 kg", "900 g", and "3 kg". Which normalisation is sound before you average it?

options.text: Convert every entry to one unit, such as grams, and average the converted numbers
Average the printed numbers as they stand, since the unit text is only a label
options.misconception: believes a unit label does not change what its number measures

options.text: Keep the largest unit in the column, since one scale suits every reading better
options.misconception: believes one unit label can substitute for converting the values

options.text: Average only the gram entries, then treat the kilogram rows as odd ones out
options.misconception: believes discarding hard rows is the same as handling them

questions.explanation: Numbers are only comparable once they share a unit. Converted to grams the three readings are 2500, 900, and 3000, which total 6400 and average 2133.3; averaged as printed they give 301.8, so the 900 gram delivery is counted as if it were 900 kilograms and the mean is inflated by a factor of about seven. The tempting answer is B, treating the unit text as decoration, which is the root cause. D looks pragmatic but silently drops half the deliveries, and a mean over the survivors describes nothing that was received.
questions.hint: Convert all three to grams and compare the two means that result.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: trace a name canonicalisation routine and count its keys
questions.stem: A cleanup routine builds one canonical key per name. DEFINE key(name): s <- name; REPLACE s, " ", ""; REPLACE s, "-", ""; s <- LOWER(s); RETURN s. The list holds "Ana Ruiz", "ana ruiz", "Ana-Ruiz", and "Bo Li". How many distinct keys does the list produce, and what are they?

options.text: 2 distinct keys, "anaruiz" and "boli"
3 distinct keys, because the two spellings of Ana stay different
options.misconception: believes lowercasing alone fails to merge the spellings

options.text: 4 distinct keys, because each raw name is treated as its own key
options.misconception: believes the routine returns the raw name rather than the key

options.text: 1 distinct key, because every row in the list is one person record
options.misconception: believes one row in a table equals exactly one person

questions.explanation: The routine strips spaces, strips hyphens, then lowercases, so "Ana Ruiz", "ana ruiz", and "Ana-Ruiz" all reduce to "anaruiz" while "Bo Li" becomes "boli". Two keys is the honest count, and the merge is the whole purpose: a group-by on the raw names would have produced four. The tempting answer is B stops one step early, noticing that two spellings differ and quitting before the case and separator steps have run.
questions.hint: Apply all three steps to each name, then count the distinct results.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: compare dates as parsed values rather than as display text
questions.stem: One log stores "2026-03-04" and another stores "March 4, 2026". What has to happen before the two can be compared?

options.text: Parse both into one fixed order with padded numbers, then compare the parsed values
Sort the strings alphabetically, since alphabetic order is calendar order
options.misconception: believes alphabetical string order matches chronological order

options.text: Compare only the year, since day and month never change a weekly total
options.misconception: believes the year alone settles any comparison of two dates

options.text: Convert both to a tool's own display format, which the application must do for you
options.misconception: believes a display format defines how a stored value orders

questions.explanation: Comparison happens on parsed values, never on display text, and a fixed padded order is what makes two strings parse to the same date. The tempting answer is B sounds reasonable until you look: "2026-03-04" sorts before "March 4, 2026" because a digit precedes a letter, which has nothing to do with time. Any tool can do the parsing, but it can only do it if the values were stored in a shape that parses, which is an encoding decision made long before the comparison.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sort order of these two strings reflects the order of the days.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: choose a stable key for removing duplicate records
questions.stem: A roster holds "Maria Gomez" twice, once as "Gomez, Maria". Which rule for removing the duplicate is sound?

options.text: Match an assigned identifier such as a household number, not the name text
Match the name with punctuation and spacing removed, since that fixes any order
options.misconception: believes tidying a name string makes it a reliable identity

options.text: Match the longest spelling, since the fullest version is the accurate record
options.misconception: believes the most complete spelling identifies the person

options.text: Keep both rows and divide every later count by two to compensate
options.misconception: believes halving the results repairs a duplicated record

questions.explanation: Identity has to come from a key that is assigned, not one that is derived from a string the person typed. Two siblings can be "Maria Gomez" and two different people can be written "Gomez, Maria", so no amount of tidying makes the name a reliable identity. The tempting answer is B is the mistake that deletes a real household from a food-bank count, and D is worse still: halving every total also halves every household that appears once, and no one notices for a year.
questions.hint: Ask which piece of data was created by the system rather than by the person.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: map spelling variants of a category to one label
questions.stem: A market count lists "apple", "apples", and "Apple". Which single cleaning rule removes the three-way split?

options.text: Map every spelling and number form to one written label chosen for that category
Delete the column, since an agreed category cannot be stored in a file
options.misconception: believes an inconsistent column is better deleted than mapped

options.text: Count the column by eye, since a human reads all three as one word
options.misconception: believes a reader's judgement counts as a stored value

options.text: Rename the file, since the file name is what splits a category three ways
options.misconception: believes a file name determines how rows are grouped

questions.explanation: Pick one label per category and map every variant to it, at entry if you can and during cleaning if you cannot. Three spellings of one fruit is not a small problem: it inflates the category count, deflates the other two, and makes the top-selling list depend on who typed the sheet. The tempting answer is C, which is exactly the shortcut that fails quietly, because the human reading it is right this time and the next spreadsheet is typed by someone else.
questions.hint: Ask what value every variant should become before any counting happens.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a percentage-point move from a relative change
questions.stem: Late-term absences at a school rise from 4% to 5%, and a headline says "absences are up 25%." What is the error?

options.text: It quotes the relative change and hides that the rate itself moved one point
It uses the wrong unit, since a rate change must be given per school day
options.misconception: believes a point move must be restated as a daily count

options.text: It quotes the wrong numbers, since 4% and 5% cannot both be correct
options.misconception: believes two valid rates cannot appear in one comparison

options.text: It is correct, because a 25% relative rise is what the numbers show
options.misconception: confuses a relative percent change with a point change

questions.explanation: A change has two honest forms and they are not interchangeable: 4% to 5% is plus one percentage point, and relative to a base of 4% it is 1 divided by 4, which is 25%. Both numbers are arithmetically right, which is exactly why the misleading move is presenting the relative figure with no point context, since a reader hearing a quarter again over a rate sitting near 4% will picture a far larger shift than the school made.
questions.hint: Compute the point change and the relative change, then see which one the headline used.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: pool rates by counts instead of averaging group rates
questions.stem: Two schools report pantry visits per 100 students. Small: 20 visits from 50 students. Large: 90 from 500. What is the pooled rate?

options.text: 110 visits from 550 students, which is 20.0 visits per 100 students
55 visits from 275 students, the two rates averaged as if sizes matched
options.misconception: averages two group rates as though the groups were equal

options.text: 20.0 per 100, because the larger school sets the rate for the district
options.misconception: lets the biggest group dictate the rate for everyone

options.text: 110 visits from 500 students, which counts the small school's students twice
options.misconception: adds visit counts while mismatching the two student totals

questions.explanation: Pool rates by adding the underlying counts, never by averaging the rates, because the groups differ in size by a factor of ten. The visits total 110 and the students total 550, so 110 divided by 550 is 0.2, which is 20.0 per 100. The tempting answer is B gives 29 per 100, since the small school's own rate is 40 and the large one's is 18, and the plain mean of those is 29: a 45% overstatement created purely by letting 50 students count as much as 500.
questions.hint: Add the counts first, then divide once to get the rate.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain how a subgroup gain can coexist with a worse overall mean
questions.stem: A food bank cuts waits in both neighbourhoods. North falls from 8 to 6 minutes on 100 weekly visits. South falls from 20 to 18 minutes as visits rise from 50 to 200. The overall mean wait still rises from 12.0 to 14.0 minutes. What explains it?

options.text: Visits shifted toward the slower neighbourhood, so the mix of cases changed the mean
One of the two neighbourhood means must have been computed with an error
options.misconception: believes subgroup gains and an overall loss cannot both be real

options.text: The overall mean is always wrong, because averaging means is never valid
options.misconception: believes any average of averages is an invalid calculation

options.text: The pattern is impossible, so at least one of the four figures is invented
options.misconception: believes the reversal is logically impossible rather than caused

questions.explanation: An overall mean mixes the groups together with whatever composition the day happened to bring, so it can move against every subgroup. Before the change, 100 times 8 plus 50 times 20 is 1800 minutes over 150 visits, which is 12.0; after, 100 times 6 plus 200 times 18 is 4200 over 300, which is 14.0. Every subgroup improved and the total rose, and the tempting answer is B assumes that a reversal this uncomfortable must be an arithmetic error rather than a real change in who is being served.
questions.hint: Recompute both overall means from the totals, then ask what changed underneath.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: supply the denominator a count-only headline is missing
questions.stem: A transit app's support page reports "complaints doubled this month." What has to be added before that sentence supports a conclusion?

options.text: The number of rides, so complaints per ride can be read from the same data
The complaint text, so readers can judge how serious each complaint was
options.misconception: believes severity text supplies the scale a rate lacks

options.text: The reporter's name, so repeat complainants can be removed next time
options.misconception: believes removing repeat complainants makes a rate honest

options.text: The exact date, so the doubling can be tied to one known event
options.misconception: believes a precise date supplies the missing denominator

questions.explanation: A bare count only becomes a rate once the population it was drawn from is stated. If rides also doubled, complaints per ride is flat; if rides grew by 20%, the complaint rate has nearly doubled. Nothing on the page tells the reader which of those is true. The tempting answer is B is a genuine kindness that does no work here, because severity changes what a complaint is worth, not how many rides produced it, and the missing quantity is a scale, not a feeling.
questions.hint: Ask what the count should be divided by before the word doubled means anything.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: trace an averaging routine that ignores group sizes
questions.stem: A report averages two group rates instead of pooling them. DEFINE meanOf(list): total <- 0; REPEAT each r IN list { total <- total + r } RETURN total / LENGTH(list). It is called with rates = [20.0, 18.0] per 100 people, and the group sizes are 50 and 500. What does the routine return, and what is the true pooled rate per 100?

options.text: 19.0, while the true pooled rate is 18.2
19.0, and the pooled rate is also 19.0 because both are means
options.misconception: believes a mean of group rates equals the pooled rate

options.text: 18.2, because LENGTH(list) divides a correct total by a wrong count
options.misconception: believes the group sizes change what a plain average returns

options.text: 38.0, because the routine divides the summed rates by one
options.misconception: believes the routine divides by the number of rates minus one

questions.explanation: The routine sums the two rates and divides by two, so 20.0 plus 18.0 is 38.0 and 38.0 divided by 2 is 19.0, and it never looks at the sizes. The pooled figure is the size-weighted average: 20 times 50 plus 18 times 500 is 10000, divided by 550, which is 18.18, and the same value comes from counts of 10 and 90 visits over 550 people. The tempting answer is B assumes averaging and pooling are the same act; they coincide only when the groups are equally large, and here the small group has the higher rate, so the gap always runs one way.
questions.hint: Trace the routine, then recompute the pooled rate as a weighted average.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a formula range from a filter selection in a total
questions.stem: A treasurer filters the ledger to last month, then runs =SUM(D2:D500) and posts the result as "last month's total" with no note. What is the flaw?

options.text: The sum reads a fixed range including hidden rows, not the rows the filter showed
The sum is slow across five hundred rows, so the figure is probably truncated
options.misconception: believes formula speed is why a reported total is untrustworthy

options.text: The sum skips blank cells, so hidden helper rows in the range pull it down
options.misconception: believes blank cells inside a range lower the value of a sum

options.text: The sum uses the wrong column, since last month's amounts live in column C
options.misconception: believes a total must be taken from the sheet's first column

questions.explanation: A formula's range defines its scope, and a filter's visible selection is not a range. Rows 2 to 500 contain every month on the sheet, so the posted total silently mixes months and reads too high, which is the sort of error that survives a year of reports. The tempting answer is C is a real curiosity that points the wrong way: a sum reads every cell in the range and adds the numbers, so blanks contribute nothing and the figure is not dragged down by them, it is dragged up by the rows nobody meant to include.
questions.hint: Ask which rows the range covers compared with which rows are visible.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why per-cell rounding makes a total drift
questions.stem: Column D holds donation weights in kilos. Column E shows =ROUND(D2,1) and looks tidy. Why can the column E total disagree with the true total?

options.text: Rounding happens per cell, so each row's small error adds up instead of cancelling
Rounding overwrites the value it reads, so the original weights are lost
options.misconception: believes a display formula replaces the value underneath it

options.text: Rounding is applied once at the end, so the total inherits a single error
options.misconception: believes rounding is deferred until the final aggregate

options.text: Display rounding changes nothing, so both totals must be identical always
options.misconception: believes rounding can never move a total at all

questions.explanation: Rounding is applied once per value, so a column of N cells can drift by roughly half a unit each and the drift accumulates. Three rows of 1.44, 1.44, and 1.45 really total 4.33, but each displays as 1.4 and the displayed column totals 4.2, so the tidy column understates the delivery by 0.13. The tempting answer is C is the intuitive model and the wrong one: rounding the total would cost one rounding, but rounding every cell first can only make the errors stack.
questions.hint: Round three sample values, then compare the sum of the rounded cells with the true sum.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: name the bias in a self-selected sample
questions.stem: A school posts a lunch survey as a QR code at the busiest till only. What does that choice do to the results?

options.text: It invites voluntary response, and one queue is not a slice of the school
It creates survivorship bias, since only students who stayed in line replied
options.misconception: labels a self-selected sample as one about who left

options.text: It creates response bias, since only spoken answers were recorded
options.misconception: confuses how answers are captured with who gets asked

options.text: It creates sampling error, since a code-based survey is less accurate
options.misconception: believes the response format itself skews who replies

questions.explanation: People who choose to answer are not a random slice: the impatient with a strong opinion and the student who just bought a hot meal are over-represented, and the queue at one till adds a time-of-day pattern on top. The tempting answer is C confuses two different things, since response bias is about how the answer is worded or recorded, while here the problem is who got the question. D is the safest-sounding and least true: a QR code is a perfectly good instrument pointed at the wrong people.
questions.hint: Ask who in the school had a chance to see the code, and who was motivated to scan.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a support inbox is not a sample of all riders
questions.stem: A transit app team surveys only the riders who emailed support, then reports the results as describing all riders. What is wrong?

options.text: The sample comes from people who already had a problem, so it over-represents them
The sample is too small, so only a larger count would settle the question
options.misconception: believes sample size alone decides representativeness

options.text: The sample is not anonymous, so people softened their answers to be polite
options.misconception: confuses response bias with who enters the sample

options.text: The sample is voluntary, since nobody was obliged to answer the email survey
options.misconception: believes every non-random sample is a voluntary response one

questions.explanation: The sample has to be drawn from the population you intend to describe. Support emailers are, by construction, people with a problem, so a claim about all riders inherits that skew however many of them reply. The tempting answer is B is the most common mistake in the whole area, treating a hundred and a thousand unlucky emails as equally useful; sample size reduces random wobble, not a selection that is wrong on purpose. D is a cousin of the real problem but a different one: nobody is obliged to reply, yet the ones who chose to were pre-filtered by having written in.
questions.hint: Ask what the emailers have in common that the general rider population does not.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish undercoverage from nonresponse
questions.stem: A food bank phones only the households it already has a number for, and about a fifth of the neighbourhood has none. What is the risk?

options.text: Undercoverage, because that fifth is missing from every result computed later
Nonresponse bias, because the uncalled households refused to take part
options.misconception: calls unreachable people the same as people who declined

options.text: Sampling error, because one fifth of a small sample is a large wobble
options.misconception: confuses a systematic coverage gap with random wobble

options.text: Response bias, because the uncalled households would answer more politely
options.misconception: believes a coverage gap shows up as politeness in answers

questions.explanation: Coverage failure and refusal are different failures with different fixes. A whole group with no reachable phone number is absent from the sampling frame, so the gap is systematic and no amount of extra calls to listed households closes it. The tempting answer is B is the sort of tidy story a team tells itself, but nobody refused anything; the number simply does not exist. And the households most likely to be unlisted are the newest arrivals, who are exactly the people the food bank most needs to hear from.
questions.hint: Ask whether the missing group refused, or was never reachable at all.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: judge when a low response rate invalidates a generalisation
questions.stem: A school invites 200 families to a survey; 60 reply. The team presents the 60 replies as representing all 200. What makes that claim unsafe?

options.text: The 140 silent families may differ from the 60 who answered, and nothing shows they do not
Sixty replies are too few for the arithmetic, so the counts must be redone
options.misconception: believes the risk is arithmetic rather than who answered

options.text: The invitations all went out in one week, so the timing skews who replied
options.misconception: believes the send window determines who chooses to reply

options.text: The survey wording is not neutral, so the phrasing of each item is at fault
options.misconception: believes representativeness depends only on question wording

questions.explanation: Below full coverage there is always an unknown gap, and non-responders usually differ from responders: families working two jobs, families without the survey's language, families with a reason to distrust the school. Nothing in the 60 replies tests that, so the generalisation rests on an assumption nobody checked. The tempting answer is B worries about arithmetic on 60 rows, which is not the fragile part; the fragile part is assuming the missing 140 behave like the 60 you can see.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence exists about the families who never replied.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: compute a share against the invited population
questions.stem: A school invites 40 families to a survey about bus punctuality. 30 reply, and 24 of those say the bus is often late. As a percentage of all 40 families invited, how many families does that represent? Give a whole number of percent.
questions.explanation: A claim about every invited family has to be divided by every invited family, so 24 out of 40 is 0.6, which is 60%. The same figure comes from the parts: 30 of 40 invited is 0.75 and 24 of 30 replies is 0.8, and 0.75 times 0.8 is 0.6. The tempting answer is 80% is true only of the families who answered, and publishing it as the school-wide figure quietly folds the 10 families who never replied into agreement they never gave.
questions.hint: Decide whether the sentence is about all invited families or only the repliers.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: predict how an absolute reference behaves when copied
questions.stem: Cell F4 holds =$C$1*B4 and the coach copies it down one row into F5. What does F5 contain?

options.text: =$C$1*B5, since the dollars lock the row and column of the first reference
=$C$2*B5, since a locked column still lets the row number move
options.misconception: confuses a locked column with a row that follows the copy

options.text: =C1*B5, because copying a formula strips every dollar sign it meets
options.misconception: believes copying removes absolute markers from a reference

options.text: =$C$1*B4, because one dollar sign freezes the whole reference
options.misconception: believes a single dollar sign locks both axes at once

questions.explanation: A dollar sign locks exactly the axis it precedes, and here both are present, so C1 does not move when the formula is copied down. The undecorated B4 has no dollars, so its row number follows the copy to 5 while its column stays B, giving =$C$1*B5. The tempting answer is B reveals the classic half-truth about dollars: they do lock a column reference, but this is a row-and-column lock, and reading it as row-only is what produces the phantom C2.
questions.hint: Check which reference carries a dollar before its row, and which carries one before its column.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: predict a division by a blank cell
questions.stem: A pantry sheet holds box counts in F2:F9 and the per-box need in G2:G9. Cell G3 is empty. What does the formula =F3/G3 display?

options.text: A division error, because an empty cell is read as zero in arithmetic
An empty cell, because a blank operand cancels itself out of the division
options.misconception: believes a blank operand is skipped instead of read as zero

options.text: The value in F3, because dividing by nothing returns the original number
options.misconception: believes division by an empty cell returns the dividend

options.text: Zero, because dividing anything by an implied zero always gives zero
options.misconception: believes division by zero returns zero instead of an error

questions.explanation: A blank cell in a formula is read as zero, and dividing by zero is undefined, so the cell shows an error rather than any number. That is why a bare division down a column with gaps is a trap: one unfilled row turns the cell red and, if the result is summed, poisons the total. The tempting answer is B is the belief that blanks are skipped, which is true of a sum and false of arithmetic, and D is a plain misconception about division that no spreadsheet makes true.
questions.hint: Decide what value the empty cell contributes, then evaluate the division.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: write a reference that reads a cell on another sheet
questions.stem: A summary sheet must read cell B7 of the sheet named Attendance. Which reference does that?

options.text: =Attendance!B7, where the sheet name and the cell address are joined by a mark
=B7, because a summary sheet reads the same address on the sheet it sits on
options.misconception: believes a cell address is global across every sheet

options.text: =Attendance.B7, because a sheet and a cell are joined by a full stop
options.misconception: believes the sheet separator is a full stop not a mark

options.text: =SUM(Attendance), because a sheet name is passed as a range to add up
options.misconception: believes naming a sheet asks for a total rather than a cell

questions.explanation: A reference that crosses sheets must name the sheet and then the address, joined by the separator the tool expects: =Attendance!B7. Typing =B7 alone reads the summary sheet's own B7, so the formula is valid, returns a number, and is quietly wrong, which is the worst kind of bug. The tempting answer is C looks like a path, and the tool rejects it outright; D is a different question, since a bare sheet name cannot be summed and belongs inside a range such as Attendance!B2:B40.
questions.hint: A cross-sheet reference needs a sheet name, a separator, and a cell.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a joined label is text, not a number
questions.stem: A roster builds a label with =B2&" - "&C2, where B2 holds 12 and C2 holds 4. What results, and what happens when a sum reads those cells?

options.text: The text "12 - 4", and a sum skips those cells because they are not numbers
The number 16, because the join sign adds the two values before joining
options.misconception: believes a join sign performs arithmetic on its operands

options.text: The text "12 - 4", and a sum reads the hyphen inside it as a minus
options.misconception: believes a hyphen in a text result is parsed as subtraction

options.text: The number 12, because a two operand join returns the first operand
options.misconception: believes a join returns its first operand unchanged

questions.explanation: The join sign builds text, so the cell holds the characters 1, 2, space, hyphen, space, 4 and a sum reading numbers skips it entirely, which drops those rows from the total with no error at all. The temptation is real, because the label looks numeric on screen, so people add it up by hand and get a different figure from the cell. The tempting answer is B is what a plus sign would have given, but the join sign was chosen precisely because no arithmetic was wanted here.
questions.hint: Decide what kind of value a text-joining formula produces, then how a sum treats it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: trace a rate routine that guards two failure cases
questions.stem: A coverage report guards a percentage twice. DEFINE rate(count, people): IF people = 0 { RETURN 0 } IF count > people { RETURN 100 } RETURN count * 100 / people. It is called on three rows in order: rate(30, 50), then rate(55, 50), then rate(0, 0). Which three values come back?

options.text: 60, then 100, then 0, one value per call in the order given
60, then 110, then 0, because the over-count guard never fires
options.misconception: believes the over-count guard does not apply to a large count

options.text: 60, then 100, then 100, because a group of zero is fully covered
options.misconception: believes an empty group means everyone was reached

options.text: 60, then 100, then an error, because the zero guard does not run
options.misconception: believes the zero denominator still reaches the division

questions.explanation: Each guard returns immediately, so only the matching one acts: 30 times 100 divided by 50 is 60; on the second call 55 is greater than 50, so the clamp returns 100 without dividing; on the third call people is 0, so the first guard returns 0 before any division happens. The tempting answer is B is what the unclamped division would give, since 55 times 100 divided by 50 is 110, and a coverage report claiming 110 percent is exactly the error the clamp exists to prevent.
questions.hint: Test each guard's condition in order and stop at the first one that holds.
